Empirical Research Plan: “Do short-term economic downturns raise the risk of civil war in sub-Saharan Africa?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) panel design with country and year fixed-effects.

Why IV is appropriate  
•  Endogenous variable: annual real GDP-per-capita growth (Δ ln yct).  
•  Measurement error and reverse causality (conflict itself depresses growth) make OLS biased.  
•  Year-to-year rainfall shocks are plausibly exogenous, highly predictive of income in rain-fed African economies, and available at high spatial resolution.  
•  Country × year panel allows us to absorb all time-invariant country factors and global shocks with two-way fixed effects.  
•  Heterogeneity questions (income, Polity, ethnic diversity, etc.) can be answered by interacting the (instrumented) growth variable with baseline characteristics.

Econometric form  

First stage:  
Δ ln yct = π1 · RainShockct  +  μc  +  λt  +  Xct β  +  εct

Second stage:  
Conflictct = α1 · Δ ln ŷct  +  μc  +  λt  +  Xct γ  +  uct

with country FE (μc), year FE (λt), and clustered SEs at the country level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
•  Δ ln ŷct = predicted real per-capita GDP growth from the first stage. A negative value represents an economic downturn.

Instrument  
•  RainShockct = (Annual rainfall in country c, year t – long-run country mean) / country s.d.  (Standardized deviation).  
  – Robustness: use % deviation, growing-season rainfall only, lagged values, GPCP vs. NCEP vs. FAOCLIM.

Control (counterfactual)  
•  Country-years that experience normal rainfall, thus no income shock, within the same country over other years and across countries in the same year once FE are partialled out.

Treatment timing  
•  Year t is “treated” if RainShockct ≤ –1 σ (severe shortfall).  In IV, the intensity of the shock is continuous.

No running variable or cutoff is required (not an RDD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance: Rainfall shocks must strongly predict GDP growth.  
  – Plausible: agriculture dominates African economies; expectation of 0.15–0.40 ppt growth per 1 σ rainfall.

A2. Exclusion Restriction: Conditional on controls/FE, rainfall affects conflict only through income.  
  – Plausible but needs discussion: rainfall could influence logistics of fighting or government capacity. See Threats section.

A3. Independence/As-if Random: Year-to-year rainfall deviations are orthogonal to unobserved determinants of conflict once μc and λt are in place.  
  – Plausible given meteorological randomness.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country rainfall spillovers on conflict).  
  – Reasonable: rainfall shocks are local; we can drop extremely small countries if worried about spatial spillovers.

A5. Correct functional form and no dynamic mis-specification.  
  – We test with lags and leads in an event-study extension.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. MAIN THREATS & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Direct (non-income) channels from rainfall to conflict  
  •  Add agricultural share × RainShockct interaction; test whether rainfall predicts conflict in non-agricultural African countries or outside Africa (placebo).  
  •  Control for rain-year length of growing season, temperature shocks, or NDVI vegetation index to capture possible logistical channels.

T2. Conflict under-reporting varies with rainfall (measurement bias)  
  •  Use multiple conflict databases (PRIO/UCDP, Fearon-Laitin, Collier-Hoeffler, Doyle-Sambanis).  
  •  Include country-specific trends in news coverage (e.g., FT article counts).

T3. Weak first stage in richer or irrigated countries → heterogeneous relevance  
  •  Report first-stage F-stats overall and by subsample.  
  •  Allow slope heterogeneity by estimating π1 separately for high-rain-dependence vs. low-rain-dependence countries.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast FE and IV
library(ivreg)      # alternative 2SLS
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#---------------------------------------------------------------
conflict <- fread("conflict_prio.csv")         # country-year conflict 0/1
rain     <- fread("rainfall_gpcp.csv")         # avg rainfall (mm)
gdp      <- fread("gdp_wb.csv")                # real GDP pc
controls <- fread("country_controls.csv")      # time-invariant & time-varying

# Merge
dat <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("iso3","year"), all=TRUE),
              list(conflict, rain, gdp, controls))

#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#---------------------------------------------------------------
setDT(dat)
# Country mean & sd rainfall over whole sample
dat[, `:=`(rain_mean = mean(rain_mm, na.rm=TRUE),
           rain_sd   =  sd(rain_mm,   na.rm=TRUE)), by = iso3]
dat[, rain_dev := (rain_mm - rain_mean)/rain_sd]           # instrument
dat[, gdp_growth := 100*(log(gdp_pc) - shift(log(gdp_pc))), by = iso3]

# Controls
dat[, ln_pop  := log(population)]
dat[, oil_exp := as.integer(oil_exporter=="yes")]

#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV regression
#---------------------------------------------------------------
fe2sls <- feols(conflict_onset ~ 1 | iso3 + year | gdp_growth ~ rain_dev,
                data = dat, cluster = ~iso3)
summary(fe2sls)

#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Heterogeneity: interact income effect with polity score
#---------------------------------------------------------------
dat[, polity_bin := as.integer(polity2 > 0)]
fe2sls_het <- feols(conflict_onset ~ polity_bin | iso3 + year |
                    gdp_growth * polity_bin ~ rain_dev * polity_bin,
                    data = dat, cluster = ~iso3)
summary(fe2sls_het)

#---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: use NCEP rainfall & alternative conflict def
#---------------------------------------------------------------
rain2 <- fread("rainfall_ncep.csv")
dat2  <- merge(dat, rain2, by=c("iso3","year"))
dat2[, rain_dev_ncep := (rain_mm_ncep - mean(rain_mm_ncep, na.rm=TRUE))/
                           sd(rain_mm_ncep, na.rm=TRUE), by = iso3]

fe2sls_rb <- feols(conflict1000 ~ 1 | iso3 + year |
                   gdp_growth ~ rain_dev_ncep,
                   data = dat2, cluster = ~iso3)
summary(fe2sls_rb)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: A negative income shock lowers the opportunity cost of rebellion and weakens state capacity → raises conflict risk.

Magnitude (prior): A 5-percentage-point fall in GDP-per-capita growth is expected to raise the probability of any civil conflict by roughly 2–3 pp (baseline mean ≈ 0.27). Elasticity ≈ −0.5 to −0.6.

Heterogeneity priors  
•  Larger effect in poor, ethnically fractionalized, and partially democratic states.  
•  Smaller (possibly zero) effect in oil exporters and highly autocratic regimes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV)  
(Coded 1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Strong first stage (F > 10)............................... 1  
C2. Exclusion restriction (no direct rain-conflict link)...... 0  
C3. No correlation of instrument with measurement error....... 1  
C4. SUTVA / no spillovers across units........................ 1  
C5. Correct functional form & dynamics properly modeled....... 0  

Overall: 3 / 5 clearly satisfied. The main open issues are the exclusion restriction and dynamics; both will be probed in robustness and placebo tests.
